about: Carve node type to ProseMirror node/mark name, for engines building a Carve <-> ProseMirror bridge. Carve type names are the node types of the spec's AST schema (resources/ast-schema.json), and every one of them has an entry in `types` or `unmapped`; the ProseMirror names are this package's CarveKit schema. Consumers read this rather than restating the mapping, which is how carve-php once ended up emitting `citation-group` against everyone else's underscores. `pm` is the name CarveKit registers; an optional `accepts` lists further names a bridge should recognize on the way in, for concepts a stock Tiptap extension already spells differently. Where two Carve types name the same ProseMirror node or mark, the one that is a vocabulary alias of the other carries `aliasOf` naming the type that owns the name; a bridge resolving a ProseMirror name back to a Carve type must not decide that by whatever order it happens to walk this file in.
attributeNaming: An attribute that carries a CARVE concept on a node or mark Tiptap already defines is spelled with a `carve` prefix (`carveRef`, `carveTight`, `carveKeyValues`), so it cannot collide with what a stock extension - or an application - puts on the same node. On a node this schema owns, the bare name is used: `carveCitation` has `raw`, not `carveRaw`. HTML-native names (`id`, `class`, `href`, `src`, `title`, `colspan`, `start`) keep their spelling wherever they appear. Two bridges to this model disagreed on every one of these before it was written down: carve-js wrote `ref`/`delim` where carve-php wrote `carveRef`/`tight`, so a document stored by one lost its reference spelling, its list tightness and its table spans when read by the other.
positionAttribute: Every block node may carry `carvePos`, the complete Carve `pos` object. Bridges use it to restore source-ordered definitions and definitions collected from emptied container lines. CarveKit retains it as non-rendered metadata.

directive.notes: a generated-content container (CARVE-P12-057): `::: toc`, `::: footnotes`, `::: bibliography`, `::: glossary`, `::: index`, `::: references`. ITS OWN NODE, deliberately not an alias of `div` the way `admonition` is. `kind` is what tells the three named-container types apart, so a bridge going back to the AST reads the type off the node instead of carrying its own copy of the six-kind enum - and cannot emit the `admonition` whose `kind` the AST schema refuses for exactly these six words. A directive's children are usually empty: its content is generated from the document, not authored between the markers

block_extension.notes: a block an extension owns (CARVE-P12-055). The REQUIRED fallback is the node's CONTENT, not an attribute: it is a real block the editor edits, and it is what the document means to a reader that does not implement the extension, so the content expression is `block` and says so. Carve 0.1 source spells none, so one reaches the editor over the AST-JSON wire only, and a canonical writer writes the fallback and reports the substitution

small_caps.notes: an interchange-only small-caps wrapper (CARVE-P12-050). A MARK, not a node: it wraps inline content and nests with every other mark, where a node would make it an atom and stop the text inside being edited. Its own attribute run does NOT ride here - CARVE-P12-050 asks a canonical writer to keep it on an ordinary attributed span around the same children, so the bridge adds a `carveSpan` mark for it and this mark carries the small-caps distinction alone. Carve 0.1 source spells no small caps, so one arrives over the AST-JSON wire only, and a canonical writer drops the wrapper, leaves the letter case alone and reports the loss

span.notes: carries id, class and extra attributes. An application that wants that registers `textStyle` itself.

preservationNodes.about: Not Carve types: the two nodes a bridge writes when it has no editable node for a construct. They are PART OF THE WIRE, not an implementation detail of one bridge - carve-grammars produced them for 179 of 1025 corpus documents and carve-php refused every one, because an unknown ProseMirror name is an error rather than a skip. A bridge reading one writes `carveSource` back as Carve source, verbatim; a bridge that cannot must say so rather than drop the node.

attrs.carveSource: the construct as written, exactly; written back verbatim
attrs.carveType: the Carve node type the atom stands in for, so a caller can say WHAT was preserved

markCarrierNodes.about: Not a Carve type either: the node a bridge writes for a MARK WITH NO CONTENT. A ProseMirror mark cannot span zero characters, and four Carve constructs parse to a mark-producing node with no children - `[](https://example.com)`, `[]{.a}`, `{++}` and `{--}`. Walking their children produces nothing, so before this node existed each one simply disappeared: a document that was only an empty-label link came back EMPTY, and nothing reported it. A bridge writes this atom instead and reads it back as the construct it names; a bridge that cannot must say so through its dropped/degraded report rather than drop the node.

attrs.markAttrs: the mark's own attributes, as one map: a link's `href`/`title` and any authored run, a span's id/class/key-values. Absent where the mark had none
attrs.markType: the ProseMirror mark this atom stands for: `link`, `carveSpan`, `carveAbbreviation`, `carveInsert`, `carveDelete`, `code` or `carveSmallCaps`. The first six have a source spelling this atom writes back; a small-caps wrapper with no children has none, so it is REPORTED as dropped rather than written
